tips.title: Fill from the middle outwards
tips.body: Put the **overlap** in first, then subtract it from each circle total to get the outer parts, then take the lot from the grand total to get the region outside. Working the other way means starting again.

tips.title: A stated circle total includes the overlap
tips.body: "19 study French" is the **whole circle**. The French-only region is $19$ minus the overlap. Writing 19 in the outer part is the single most common error here.

tips.title: Given that changes the denominator
tips.body: An ordinary probability divides by the **grand total**. A **conditional** one, signalled by *given that*, divides by the **circle total** instead. Decide which before writing the fraction.

tips.title: Start in the overlap
tips.body: Fill the **intersection** first, then work outwards by subtracting it from each circle total. Going the other way makes the circle-only regions too big, because a stated circle total always **includes** the overlap that has not been taken off yet.

why.matters:
Venn diagrams exist because **groups overlap, and overlapping groups cannot be added up**. Count the people who do one thing, count the people who do another, add the two, and anyone who does both has been counted twice.

The diagram is a way of holding four separate quantities — only this, only that, both, neither — where adding them is safe. The "neither" region is the one people forget, and it is usually the one the question is about.

examples.title: The overlap you counted twice
examples.body:
In a class of 30, 18 play football and 15 play cricket. How many play neither?

18 plus 15 is 33, which is more than the class. Nobody has miscounted: the 8 people who play both have been counted in each list. Take the overlap off once and 25 play at least one, so 5 play neither.

The four regions are 10 football only, 7 cricket only, 8 both and 5 neither, and those do add to 30. Every survey you have ever seen quoted has this problem underneath it — the percentages in a "what do people use" chart add to well over 100 for exactly this reason, and it is not an error.

visual.alt: A two circle Venn diagram inside a rectangle, with ten in the football only region, seven in cricket only, eight in the overlap and five outside both circles

steps.title: What the regions mean
steps.body:
A **Venn diagram** sorts things into overlapping sets. Each circle is one set, the rectangle round the outside is everything being considered, and every single item sits in **exactly one region**.

That last point is the whole trick. The number written inside the overlap is the number in **both**. The number written in the rest of circle A is the number in **A but not B**, not the total for A.

So when a question says "19 study French", that 19 is the **whole circle**, and it has to be split between the overlap and the part outside it. Filling a diagram nearly always means working **inwards to outwards**: put the overlap in first, then subtract.

The rectangle is called the **universal set**, written $\xi$. The region inside the rectangle but outside every circle is the one students forget, and it is where a mark usually hides.

visuals.alt: A Venn diagram of thirty students studying French or Spanish, with twelve studying French only, seven both, five Spanish only and six neither
Four boxes about reading a Venn diagram: the overlap, the part of a circle outside it, the region outside every circle, and the universal set rectangle

steps.title: Filling one in, from the middle outwards
steps.body:
Here is the question that produced the diagram above. **30 students** were asked which languages they study. **19** study French, **12** study Spanish, and **7** study both.

Notice what those numbers are: 19 and 12 are **whole circles**, and they overlap. Adding them gives 31, which is more than 30, because the 7 in both have been counted twice. Filling the diagram fixes that automatically.

steps.body: Once the diagram is filled, a probability is just a region divided by the total. The denominator is the number in the **rectangle**, not the number in a circle.

check.prompt: Of 30 students, 12 study French only, 7 study both French and Spanish, 5 study Spanish only and 6 study neither. What is the probability that a student chosen at random studies neither language? Give your answer as a fraction or a decimal.
check.solution: $6$ students are outside both circles, so $P = \dfrac{6}{30} = \dfrac{1}{5} = 0.2$.

steps.title: Three sets
steps.body:
Three circles make **eight** regions: three for one set only, three for exactly two sets, one for all three, and the outside.

The method does not change, but the order matters more: **start in the very middle and work outwards**. Fill all three, then the pairs, then the singles, then the outside. Going the other way means redoing it.

Watch the wording of what you are given. "15 play A and B" usually means the whole overlap of A and B, which **includes** the ones who play all three. So the A-and-B-only region is $15$ minus the middle.

check.prompt: In a three set Venn diagram, 12 people are in both A and B, and 4 people are in all three sets. How many are in A and B but not C?
check.solution: The 12 in both A and B includes the 4 in all three, so A and B but not C is $12 - 4 = 8$.

steps.title: Conditional probability from a Venn diagram
steps.body:
A **conditional** probability restricts the people you are choosing from. "Given that she studies French" means the French circle is now the whole world, so the **denominator changes**.

This is the single most common Higher tier Venn question, and the whole of it is: use the circle total, not the grand total.

check.solution: The Spanish circle holds $12$ students and $7$ of them also study French, so $P = \dfrac{7}{12}$.

steps.title: Your turn: fill it in, then read it
steps.body:
Sixty people were asked about two streaming services. **38** use A, **27** use B, and **14** use both.

1. Fill in the four regions. Start with the overlap.
2. Check the four regions add to 60.
3. Find $P(\text{uses neither})$.
4. A person is chosen from those who use A. Find the probability they also use B.

The last one has a different denominator from the others. Say which, and why.

check.prompt: Sixty people were asked about two streaming services. 38 use A, 27 use B and 14 use both. How many use neither?
check.solution: A only is $38 - 14 = 24$ and B only is $27 - 14 = 13$. Inside the circles that is $24 + 14 + 13 = 51$, so neither is $60 - 51 = 9$.

steps.title: Going deeper: notation, and working backwards
steps.body:
**The notation.** Edexcel writes Venn questions with set notation, and reading it is free marks.

- $\xi$ is the **universal set**: everything in the rectangle.
- $A \cap B$ is the **intersection**: in A **and** B, the overlap. The symbol has a roof on it, like the A in *and*.
- $A \cup B$ is the **union**: in A **or** B or both, the whole of both circles.
- $A'$ is the **complement**: everything **not** in A, including the outside region.
- $n(A)$ means **how many** are in A, while $P(A)$ is a probability.

So $n(A \cap B')$ is the number in A but not B, which is the A-only region.

**Working backwards.** The hardest form gives you a probability and asks for a missing number. Write the region you want over the total as an equation and solve it. If $P(\text{both}) = \dfrac{1}{5}$ out of 30, then the overlap is $\dfrac{1}{5} \times 30 = 6$, and the rest of the diagram follows.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Each region of a Venn diagram holds the items in **exactly** that region, so the overlap is **both** and the rest of a circle is **that set only**.
- Fill in from the **middle outwards**: overlap first, then the singles, then the outside.
- A number like "19 study French" is a **whole circle**, so subtract the overlap to get the French-only region.
- Always check the regions add to the total in the rectangle.
- For a probability, the denominator is the **total in the rectangle**, and that includes the people outside every circle.
- For a **conditional** probability, the denominator becomes the **circle total** instead.
- Three sets give eight regions. "A and B" usually includes the ones in all three, so subtract the middle.
- Notation: $\xi$ universal set, $\cap$ intersection (and), $\cup$ union (or), $A'$ not A, $n(A)$ a count.
- This diagram: French only 12, both 7, Spanish only 5, neither 6, total 30.

questions.prompt: In a class of 25, 14 play football, 9 play tennis and 5 play both. How many play tennis only?
questions.solution: The tennis circle totals 9 and 5 of those also play football, so tennis only is $9 - 5 = 4$.

questions.prompt: In a class of 25, 14 play football, 9 play tennis and 5 play both. How many play neither?
questions.solution: Football only is 9, both is 5 and tennis only is 4, so $9 + 5 + 4 = 18$ are inside the circles. Neither is $25 - 18 = 7$.

questions.prompt: What does the rectangle around a Venn diagram represent?
questions.solution: The rectangle is the **universal set**, written $\xi$. The region inside it but outside every circle holds the items in neither set.
options: The universal set: everything being considered
The items in both sets
The larger of the two sets
The items in neither set

questions.prompt: A Venn diagram shows 19 in the French circle altogether and 7 in the overlap. What number goes in the French-only part?
questions.solution: The whole circle is 19 and the overlap is 7, so the French-only part is $19 - 7 = 12$.

questions.prompt: From a group of 30 students, 12 study French only, 7 study both, 5 study Spanish only and 6 study neither. What is the probability a student chosen at random studies both? Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.
questions.solution: $7$ of the $30$ students are in the overlap, so $P = \dfrac{7}{30}$.

questions.prompt: Of 30 students, 12 study French only, 7 study both French and Spanish, 5 study Spanish only and 6 study neither. What is the probability that a student chosen at random studies at least one of the two languages? Give your answer as a fraction or a decimal.
questions.solution: $24$ students are inside a circle, so $P = \dfrac{24}{30} = \dfrac{4}{5} = 0.8$. Or use $1 - \dfrac{6}{30}$.

questions.prompt: In a three set Venn diagram, 15 people are in both A and B, and 6 are in all three. How many are in A and B but not C?
questions.solution: The 15 in both A and B includes the 6 in all three, so $15 - 6 = 9$ are in A and B but not C.

questions.solution: X only is $22 - 9 = 13$ and Y only is $18 - 9 = 9$. Inside the circles that is $13 + 9 + 9 = 31$, so neither is $40 - 31 = 9$.

questions.solution: 'Given they study French' makes the French circle the whole sample, and it holds $19$ students. $7$ of them also study Spanish, so $P = \dfrac{7}{19}$.

questions.solution: Exactly one means the three outer single regions: $8 + 7 + 2 = 17$. The pairs and the middle are excluded.

questions.solution: The overlap is $\dfrac{1}{5}$ of the total: $\dfrac{1}{5} \times 30 = 6$.

questions.prompt: In a class of 32, 20 study art, 15 study music and 4 study neither. How many study both?
questions.solution: Inside the circles there are $32 - 4 = 28$. Adding the circles gives $20 + 15 = 35$, which counts the overlap twice, so the overlap is $35 - 28 = 7$.

questions.prompt: Sixty people were asked which of two streaming services they use. 38 use A, 27 use B and 14 use both. Draw the Venn diagram and find the probability that a person chosen at random uses neither.
questions.solution: The overlap is 14, since that is the number using both. The A circle totals 38, so A only is 38 minus 14, which is 24. The B circle totals 27, so B only is 27 minus 14, which is 13. Inside the circles altogether that is 24 plus 14 plus 13, which is 51. The total is 60, so the number using neither is 60 minus 51, which is 9. The probability of using neither is therefore 9 out of 60, which cancels to 3 over 20, or 0.15.

markScheme.description: puts 14 in the overlap and subtracts to get 24 and 13

criteria.text: Puts 14 in the overlap and works outwards to 24 and 13
Finds 9 in the region outside both circles
Gives the probability as 9/60, cancelled to 3/20 or 0.15

questions.modelAnswer:
**Fill from the middle.** Both is **14**.

- A only $= 38 - 14 = \mathbf{24}$
- B only $= 27 - 14 = \mathbf{13}$

**Inside the circles** $= 24 + 14 + 13 = 51$.

**Outside** $= 60 - 51 = \mathbf{9}$.

**Check:** $24 + 14 + 13 + 9 = 60$. ✓

$$P(\text{neither}) = \dfrac{9}{60} = \dfrac{3}{20} = 0.15$$

questions.prompt: Of 30 students, 12 study French only, 7 study both French and Spanish, 5 study Spanish only and 6 study neither. Explain why the probability that a student studies Spanish is not the same as the probability that a student studies Spanish given that they study French, and work out both.
questions.solution: The first probability is taken from the whole group, so its denominator is 30, the number in the rectangle. The Spanish circle holds 12 students, so the probability a student studies Spanish is 12 over 30. The second probability is conditional: being told the student studies French means the choice is now only from inside the French circle, so the denominator changes to 19, the number of French students. Of those 19, the 7 in the overlap also study Spanish, so the probability is 7 over 19. The two differ because the condition shrinks the group being chosen from, which changes the denominator and usually changes the answer.

markScheme.description: the condition changes the denominator to 19
explains that the condition restricts the group chosen from

criteria.text: Explains that the condition restricts the choice to the French circle
Gives P(Spanish given French) as 7 out of 19
Explains clearly that the denominator changes, which is why the two differ

questions.modelAnswer:
**The ordinary probability** is taken from the whole group, so the denominator is **30**, the number in the rectangle. The Spanish circle holds 12 students:

$$P(\text{Spanish}) = \dfrac{12}{30} = \dfrac{2}{5}$$

**The conditional probability** is different. Being told the student studies French means we are only choosing from **inside the French circle**, which holds $12 + 7 = 19$ students. Of those, the **7** in the overlap also study Spanish:

$$P(\text{Spanish} \mid \text{French}) = \dfrac{7}{19}$$

**Why they differ.** The condition **shrinks the group being chosen from**, so the denominator changes from 30 to 19. Only the students who study French are still in the running, and a different denominator gives a different answer.

questions.solution: The whole football circle is its four regions: $8 + 5 + 4 + 3 = 20$.

examTechnique.body:
Fill the diagram in before you answer anything. Even when the question asks for one number, the diagram is where the method marks are.

**Middle outwards, every time.** Overlap first, then the singles by subtraction, then the outside region from the total. Going the other way means starting again.

Remember that a stated circle total **includes** the overlap. "19 study French" is the whole circle, so French only is $19 - 7$.

Check your regions add to the total in the rectangle. That catches almost every arithmetic slip.

For a probability, the denominator is the **rectangle total** unless the question says *given that*, in which case it becomes the **circle total**. Deciding which before you write the fraction is the difference between full marks and none.

Learn the five symbols. $\xi$, $\cap$, $\cup$, $A'$ and $n(A)$ appear in the question, not in the answer, so not reading them costs marks before you start.
examinerErrors: Putting the whole circle total in the circle-only region instead of subtracting the overlap.
Leaving out the region inside the rectangle but outside every circle, so the total is wrong.
Using a circle total as the denominator for an ordinary probability instead of the grand total.
Using the grand total for a conditional probability, when *given that* changes the denominator to the circle total.
On three sets, treating "A and B" as the pair-only region when it includes the ones in all three.
Confusing ∪ with ∩. Union is or, intersection is and.
Answering n(A) with a probability, or P(A) with a count.
Not checking that the regions add back to the total.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer fills the diagram from the middle outwards without being told to, and checks the regions against the total before going on. It knows a stated circle total includes the overlap, and on three sets it subtracts the middle from each pair. It reads the set notation, so $n(A \cap B')$ is answered with a count and $P(A \cup B)$ with a fraction. Above all it spots *given that* and changes the denominator to the circle total, and can explain in words why the condition makes the answer different.
